title: Baseline Characteristics of Participants in STAREE: A Randomized Trial for Primary Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease Events and Prolongation of Disability‐Free Survival in Older People
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association: Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Disease

sections.abstract:
The risk–benefit balance of statin use in healthy older people is uncertain. We describe the baseline characteristics of the STAREE (Statins in Reducing Events in the Elderly) trial, which is a randomized, double‐blind, placebo‐controlled trial among community‐dwelling older people; the trial evaluated the effect of atorvastatin 40 mg for the prevention of major cardiovascular events (cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction or stroke), and on disability‐free survival (survival free of both dementia and persistent physical disability).

STAREE enrolled people aged ≥70 years from 1583 general practices across Australia with no history of clinical cardiovascular disease, diabetes, or dementia. Baseline data collected included demographic, clinical, cognitive (Modified Mini‐Mental State Examination), psychological (Center for Epidemiologic Studies Short Depression Scale), lifestyle, medical, physical, blood and urine measures, and quality of life. Demographic and clinical characteristics of study participants were then compared with publicly available landmark statin trials. A total of 9971 participants were recruited (mean±SD age 74.7±4.5 years, 4023 (40%) ≥75 years, 52% women) between July 2015 and March 2023. The mean low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol was 3.27 mmol/L (SD=0.72; 126 mg/dL). Hypertension was reported by 43% of participants and the mean blood pressure was 136/80 mm Hg. Compared with previous landmark statin trials that included primary prevention cohorts, STAREE is unique in including such a large number of older (≥75 years) independent‐living people.

STAREE is the largest primary prevention trial of statins powered to address the important clinical outcomes of major cardiovascular events, disability‐free survival, and cognition in older people.

https://www.clinicaltrials.gov ; Unique identifier: NCT02099123 .

Keywords: primary prevention, randomized clinical trial, statins

Subject Categories: Primary Prevention, Aging, Cardiovascular Disease, Complications, Vascular Disease
sections.methods:
The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.

The study design and sample size calculation of STAREE have been previously described. 2 Briefly, STAREE is a double‐blind, placebo‐controlled, randomized primary prevention trial examining the effects of statin therapy on 2 co‐primary clinical end points: (1) a composite of all‐cause death or dementia or development of persistent physical disability; and (2) a composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction or nonfatal stroke in healthy older people. STAREE participants were randomized 1:1 to oral 40 mg atorvastatin or matching placebo to have 80% statistical power to detect a 20% reduction in major cardiovascular events and 83% power to detect 14.5% reduction in first occurrence of dementia, persistent disability, or death. The STAREE steering committee developed the protocol and operational plan after consultation with consumers and general practitioner co‐investigators. The protocol was approved by the human research ethics committees/institutional review boards of Monash University (primary site, Project ID 2787 and 21528), Royal Australian College of General Practice (14‐017), Curtin University Human Research Ethics Committee (HR113/2015), Tasmanian Health and Medical Research Ethics Committee (H0014918), and University of Newcastle Human Research Ethics Committee (H‐2016‐0266). 2 A Data and Safety Monitoring Board provides independent governance oversight. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT02099123 .

Participants were enrolled from 1583 registered General Practices across metropolitan and regional/rural Australia. Adults 70 years and older without a history of CVD events (defined as myocardial infarction, angina, coronary artery angioplasty and/or stenting, coronary artery bypass grafting surgery, heart failure, stroke, transient ischemic attack, carotid stenosis, abdominal, aortic aneurysm and peripheral vascular disease), diabetes, dementia or other life‐limiting conditions, and living independently were identified from general practice clinical databases as eligible for the study. All participants provided written informed consent.

Key inclusion and exclusion criteria are shown in Table 1 . Potential participants underwent an initial phone screening for trial inclusion and exclusion criteria. Those who were eligible were then invited to take part in 2 baseline screening visits separated by a 4‐week run‐in period, either as a face‐to‐face visit at their usual general practitioner clinic or as a remote phone visit with a trained study team member. This included accessing recent or requesting additional laboratory assessments via their usual general practitioner. Eligible, consenting participants were randomized after the second baseline visit.

STAREE Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria

STAREE indicates Statins in reducing events in the elderly.

In response to social isolation requirements due to the COVID‐19 pandemic, an abridged version of the 3MS was used that excluded items that were inapplicable for telephone administration.

Details regarding data collection methodology have been previously presented. 2 Briefly, participants self‐completed surveys providing details of their health and medical history. Participants were asked to self‐identify their race from the following categories: White/Caucasian, Asian, Aboriginal/Torres Strait Islander, Pacific Islander or Maori, African, “more than one race” or “unknown or not reported.” Medication use was based on either self‐report over the telephone or directly observed on clinic visits. Fasting blood and urine results were obtained via the participant's local general practitioner.

The characteristics of participants were grouped as follows: clinical, cognitive, and psychological characteristics and physical, blood, and urinary characteristics. Cognition was measured using the Modified Mini Mental State Examination 27 and, in response to social isolation requirements due to the COVID‐19 pandemic, an abridged version of the Modified Mini Mental State Examination, which excluded items that were inapplicable for telephone administration. The Center for Epidemiologic Studies Short Depression Scale 28 was used to identify depressive symptoms, and the SF‐6D, derived from the Short Form‐36, 29 was used to measure health utility quality of life.

Descriptive summary statistics including mean and SD for approximately normally distributed variables, median and interquartile range (IQR) for variables following a skewed distribution, or n (%) were used as appropriate to describe participants' baseline characteristics at completion of study recruitment (in early 2023) and without knowledge of the randomization assignment. Summary statistics were calculated for all participants and also within prespecified subgroups of interest: sex (man, woman), age group (70–74 years, ≥75 years), and urbanization of geographical region of participant residence (metropolitan, regional/remote). Medications were categorized according to the World Health Organization Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical classification system. 30 Statistical analyses were performed using Stata version 16.1 (StataCorp, College Station, TX).

Publicly available summary statistics describing the relevant characteristics of comparable Australians at the population level were obtained from a variety of sources such as the Australian Bureau of Statistics, 31 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 32 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care, 33 and the Australian Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme 34 using the most recently published data.
sections.results:
A total of 22 305 people were screened between August 2015 and February 2023 (Table S1 provides the names of all general practitioners involved). The number of people randomized into the trial across time once deemed eligible on telephone screening before, during, and following the social isolation requirements of the COVID‐19 pandemic are summarized in Table S2 . During the social isolation requirements of the COVID‐19 pandemic, the number of annual screening phone calls decreased but the ratio of randomization to screening remained similar. The number of people at each step of the recruitment process over the entire recruitment period is shown in the Figure . Following 2 screening visits and a 4‐week placebo‐only run in‐phase, a total of 9971 people were randomized. The most common reasons for failing to progress past the screening phase were exclusion due to 1 or more of the criteria listed in Table 1 (n=6583) or declining further participation (n=5299). Compared with the eligible and willing cohort, the randomized cohort was of similar age and sex distribution (Table S3 ).

*Reasons include: participant taking statin at time of screening, use of contraindicated concomitant medication and not meeting functional independence criteria. † Reasons include: failure to adhere to study compliance run‐in period, unable to be contacted for further involvement, and missing final recruitment timeframe cut‐off. CONSORT indicates Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials; GP, general practitioner; and STAREE, Statins in Reducing Events in the Elderly.

The baseline characteristics of randomized participants are presented in Table 2 . The mean (SD) age of participants at randomization was 74.7 (4.5) years, with 40% of participants ≥75 years of age. Women made up 52% of participants and 41% resided in a regional/remote area. Most participants were White and spoke English as their primary language (>95%). Over half of participants had completed tertiary education (54%). Most participants reported current alcohol use (>80%) and never smoking (55%). Almost half (43%) reported a history of hypertension. The median number of medications reported by participants to be taken regularly was 2 (IQR:1–4) with 20% taking at least 5 medications. The most commonly used medications were blood pressure lowering agents (46%) followed by those for acid‐related gastrointestinal disorders (27%) and analgesia (21%). Less than 1% of participants reported previously taking a lipid‐lowering agent.

Clinical, Cognitive, and Psychological Characteristics by Age at Randomization

CESD‐10 indicates Center for Epidemiological Studies Depression Scale; 3MS, Modified Mini‐Mental State Test (x/100); Modified 3MS, telephone modified 3MS (x/73); SF‐6D, Short‐Form Six‐Dimension; and STAREE, Statins in Reducing Events in the Elderly. Cancer defined as self‐reported history of diagnosis of cancer, excluding nonmelanomatous skin cancer.

The median Center for Epidemiologic Studies Short Depression Scale score (score ≥16/30 indicative of risk of clinical depression) of participants was 3 (IQR:1–6) and ≈9% had a score ≥10. 35 The median Modified Mini Mental State Examination score was 95 (IQR: 91–97) (score <78/100 warranting further screening for cognitive impairment or dementia 27 ) in those assessed face to face (n=8924) and 70/73 (IQR: 67–71) in those assessed using the telephone Modified Mini Mental State Examination (n=1047).

Compared with participants <75 years of age, those ≥75 years (n=4023, 40%) more often reported living alone (33% versus 21%), having hypertension (48% versus 40%), and polypharmacy (taking ≥5 medications) (23% versus 17%) (Table 2 ). Those ≥75 years of age reported lower quality of life than those <75 years (median Short‐Form Six‐Dimension: 0.70 versus 0.74) (score closer to 0 indicating better quality of life 29 ). Compared with men, women more often reported living alone (33% versus 18%), experiencing muscle symptoms (51% versus 41%), polypharmacy (25% versus 15%), not completing tertiary education (51% versus 41%), no current alcohol use (21% versus 14%), and never smoking (62% versus 47%) (Table S4 ). Those living in regional/rural areas had similar characteristics as those living in metropolitan areas. However, the prevalence of hypertension and polypharmacy was slightly greater in those living in regional/rural areas than in metropolitan areas (hypertension: 46% versus 41%; polypharmacy: 23% versus 18%) (Table S5 ).

Table 3 presents the baseline physical, fasting blood, and urinary measures of trial participants. The median total cholesterol of participants was 5.5 mmol/L (IQR: 4.9–6.0) (213 mg/dL), the median high‐density lipoprotein cholesterol was 1.5 mmol/L (IQR: 1.3–1.8) (58 mg/dL), and the mean low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol was 3.27 mmol/L (SD=0.72) (126 mg/dL). The median body mass index (BMI) of participants was 27.0 (IQR: 24.3–30.1) with 26% categorized as “obese” (BMI >30 kg/m 2 ). The mean blood pressure of participants was 136/80 mm Hg.

Baseline Physical and Pathology Measures Overall and by Age at Randomization

Compared with participants <75 years of age, those ≥75 years were broadly similar with regard to BMI, blood pressure, cholesterol levels, triglycerides, and liver and renal function. Women had lower BMI, waist circumference, and blood pressure than men but had higher total cholesterol, low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol, and high‐density lipoprotein cholesterol (Table S6 ). The characteristics of participants living in metropolitan areas were similar to those living in regional/rural areas with the exception of BMI, with those living in regional/rural areas having a slightly higher mean BMI than those living in metropolitan areas and a greater proportion within the obese BMI range (28% versus 24%) (Table S7 ).

The proportion of women enrolled in the STAREE trial (52%) reflects the broader Australian population >65 years of age (53%). 32 However, STAREE participants had a higher rate of speaking English as a first language than the general Australian >65 years population (96% versus 82%). 32 The proportion reporting living alone was similar among STAREE participants (26%) and those >65 years of age in Australia (25%) as was the proportion living in regional/remote areas (41% versus 45%). 36 The proportion of STAREE participants who were overweight was greater than in the Australian population (42% versus 34%) but the proportion in the obese category was lower (26% versus 32%). Although the prevalence of hypertension among STAREE participants (43%) was similar to that among similarly aged Australians (39%), 31 the prevalence of cardiometabolic risk factors was much lower, reflective of the STAREE trial's focus on primary prevention.
sections.discussion:
This article describes the baseline characteristics of almost 10 000 older people across Australia successfully recruited into a primary prevention trial of atorvastatin versus placebo with excellent representation of older people from metropolitan, regional, and remote communities. Compared with previous landmark statin trials, the baseline characteristics of participants in our trial demonstrate that it is the first statin trial to include such a large number of people aged >70 and >75 years with near equal and proportional sex representation. On entry, participants were living independently and reflect older people who could potentially benefit from statin (atorvastatin) treatment to extend life span free of dementia, disability, and major CVD.

Previous primary prevention trials have tended to include few older people aged >70 years of (Table 4 ). 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 Despite the well‐recognized greater proportion of women in older society, most previous primary prevention trials have enrolled lower proportions of women than STAREE with the exception of the Prospective Study of Pravastatin in the Elderly at Risk (PROSPER) trial (52%) 21 and the Mangement of Elevated Cholesterol in the Primary Prevention Group of Adult Japanese (MEGA) trials (68%). 24 Indeed, 1 early trial excluded women. 18 Such under‐representation of these important groups that represent a large proportion of our aging society has been highlighted by the evidence gap identified by the most recent Cholesterol Treatment Trialists Collaboration meta‐analysis 3 regarding the role of statins in those aged ≥75 years of age.

Consistent with previously published work, 31 , 32 we found that the oldest people in our trial were more likely to live alone, have lower quality of life, and take more medications. Similarly, the well‐described pattern for women to be more to likely to have depression than men 37 is reflected in the higher Center for Epidemiologic Studies Short Depression Scale scores of women and may potentially explain the greater medication use by women than men in our study.

This study has a number of strengths. STAREE will assess the effect of statin on disability‐free survival as well as first CVD event in a large, older population. This has an advantage over previous trials that tended to focus on CVD in isolation (Table 4 ), potentially missing end points that are highly relevant to older people. The agent choice of atorvastatin at a dose of 40 mg also has an advantage over older studies that have used less potent statins such as simvastatin and pravastatin (Table 4 ). 13 Atorvastatin 40 mg is comparable in expected low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol lowering to that of the most recent trials, with an expected low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol reduction of 30–50%. 13 This expected reduction avoids the greater risks of adverse events associated with higher doses of alternate agents such as simvastatin ≥80 mg. 13 , 38 , 39 The regular collection of detailed data regarding cognition and other symptoms that had been associated with statin use (but with unclear causal links) will also address patients' and prescribing clinicians' concerns as to the risks associated with statin use in older people.

STAREE also has limitations. Despite a highly decentralized recruitment strategy through Australian general practices, participants are predominantly White and English‐speaking. Other studies, such as the ongoing Pragmatic evaluation of events and benefits of lipid lowering in older adults (PREVENTABLE) Trial 40 in the United States with an emphasis on recruiting Black/African‐American and Hispanic/Latinx participants should provide further clarity and guidance in diverse populations.
sections.conclusion: STAREE represents the largest primary prevention trial to date of statins in healthy older people to reduce the risk of major cardiovascular events and a composite of death, dementia, or development of persistent physical disability. STAREE's cohort characteristics suggest that the results of the trial will have strong external validity. STAREE will provide crucial evidence on the role of statins to optimize CVD, disability‐free survival, and cognition in older people.
